title: Determining the appropriate number of particles on a filter to allow small microplastics to be analyzed by microscopy
author: Xu, Arakawa

steps.title: Prepare circular filter
steps.instruction: Use a circular filter of 12.2 mm diameter; a double‑layer hole structure with 20 µm pores is recommended, although the simulation assumes all particles are retained regardless of pore size.

steps.title: Measure sample particle characteristics
steps.instruction: After oxidation treatment and density separation, determine the particle concentration (particles · mL⁻¹) and the particle‑size distribution of the subsample that will be used for microscopy.

steps.title: Install particle‑distribution simulator
steps.instruction: Install Python 3.7.3 and the required packages: PyQt5‑Qt 5.15.2 (GUI toolkit), NumPy 1.20.3 (data analysis), and Matplotlib 3.1.0 (plotting). Launch the GUI titled “particle distribution simulator”.

substeps.instruction: Only digits are accepted in the diameter column; only integers are accepted in the number column.
If a non‑numeric entry is made, an error message appears.
Press the ‘Apply’ button to run the simulation, ‘Image Save’ to export the plot, and ‘Quit’ to close the program.

steps.title: Set simulation parameters
steps.instruction: In the GUI, input the desired particle size(s) (µm) and particle number(s). Use the loop numbers 10, 50, 100, 500, 1 000, 5 000, 10 000, 20 000; the validation showed that 500 loops give a stable isolation ratio, so select 500 loops for all subsequent runs.

substeps.instruction: Particle sizes tested in the study were 50, 100 and 150 µm.

steps.title: Run simulation and obtain isolation ratio
steps.instruction: Press ‘Apply’; the program randomly distributes the specified particles on a virtual 12.2 mm circular filter (coordinates to eight decimal places, particles are circles with aspect ratio 1, no particles extend beyond the filter edge). The isolation ratio (%) is calculated as IsolationRatio = (IsolatedParticles / AllParticles) × 100, where an isolated particle has no overlap or tangential contact with any other particle.

steps.title: Determine particle density for 99 % isolation
steps.instruction: Use the empirical equation D = 4.13 e^(‑0.02 S) (R² = 0.862, p < 0.05) where D is the particle density (particles · mm⁻²) that yields an isolation ratio of 99 % and S is particle size in µm. Compute D for each relevant size (e.g., S = 25 µm → D ≈ 5.13 mm⁻²; S = 100 µm → D ≈ 0.351 mm⁻²).

steps.title: Calculate maximum particles per filter
steps.instruction: Calculate the filter area: A = π × (d/2)² = π × (12.2 mm / 2)² ≈ 117 mm². Multiply the density D (particles · mm⁻²) by A to obtain the maximum total number of particles that can be placed on the filter while maintaining ≥99 % isolation.

steps.title: Allocate particles according to sample distribution
steps.instruction: Apply the measured size‑distribution ratio of the real sample to the total particle number calculated in the previous step. For example, a Tokyo Bay sample had a ratio 60 µm : 80 µm : 100 µm : 120 µm : >130 µm = 7 : 2.95 : 3.05 : 1 : 1; particles >130 µm were treated as 200 µm. If the total allowable particles on the filter are 60, distribute them proportionally (27 : 11 : 13 : 4 : 5 particles respectively).

steps.title: Calculate sample volume to filter
steps.instruction: Using the particle concentration measured in step 2, compute the volume of the original sample that contains the allocated number of particles for each size class. This volume is the amount to be passed through the filter.

steps.title: Perform vacuum filtration
steps.instruction: Place the prepared 12.2 mm filter in the vacuum filtration apparatus and filter the calculated sample volume. Ensure the vacuum does not disturb particle placement on the filter.

steps.title: Microscopy analysis
steps.instruction: After filtration, examine the filter under the microscope. Because the isolation ratio is ≥99 %, overlapping particles should be negligible, allowing accurate counting and sizing of microplastics.
